mcqs.question: A system has an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 2 hours. What does this mean?
options: After a disaster, at most 5 minutes of data is lost, and the system must be back up within 2 hours
It takes 5 minutes to fail over and 2 hours to lose data
The system backs up every 2 hours and can tolerate 5 minutes of downtime
RPO and RTO here mean the same thing measured two different ways
mcqs.explanation: RPO bounds acceptable data loss (5 minutes' worth here) and RTO bounds acceptable downtime (2 hours here) — they're independent metrics, not two versions of the same measurement, and the option reversing which number applies to data loss vs downtime is wrong.

mcqs.question: A system uses continuous replication to a standby that only exists as a cold backup file, rebuilt from scratch on failure. What's true about its RPO and RTO?
options: Both RPO and RTO will be excellent, since continuous replication covers both
RPO will be good (near-zero data loss) but RTO will be poor, since rebuilding infrastructure from scratch takes real time regardless of data freshness
RPO will be poor but RTO will be good
Continuous replication makes RTO irrelevant as a metric
mcqs.explanation: Continuous replication controls data freshness (RPO), not how fast new infrastructure can be stood up and promoted (RTO) — a cold rebuild is slow no matter how current the underlying data is. RTO stays a fully relevant, separate metric.

mcqs.question: A business says losing up to a day of data and being down for a few hours during a rare disaster is acceptable. Which approach best fits, avoiding overspend?
options: Continuous replication with a warm standby
Periodic snapshot every 15 minutes with a warm standby
Nightly backup with a cold rebuild
Continuous replication with a cold rebuild
mcqs.explanation: A day of tolerable data loss and hours of tolerable downtime map directly to nightly backup plus cold rebuild — the cheapest option that still meets both stated requirements. The other approaches all buy tighter RPO or RTO than the business asked for, at higher steady-state cost.

mcqs.question: A team has a detailed, well-written disaster-recovery runbook that has never been executed, even in a drill. What should you conclude about their actual RPO and RTO?
options: They match whatever the runbook states, since the document defines the numbers
They are automatically worse than any tested plan by a fixed factor
RPO and RTO don't require drills to verify, only good documentation
They are unknown — an unrehearsed runbook is an untested hypothesis, and real failovers routinely surface problems a document doesn't predict
mcqs.explanation: A runbook's stated numbers are aspirational until executed — expired permissions, stale scripts, and forgotten dependencies are exactly the kind of thing only a real rehearsal surfaces. There's no fixed penalty factor to apply, and documentation alone can't substitute for actually running the procedure.
